title: Flawed solution unjustified
statement: How many positive integers $n$ are such that $n + 30$ divides $n^2 + 300$?
hints: Compare $n$ with $n + 30$: what is $n^2 + 300$ close to?
Reduce modulo $n + 30$: the remainder is a constant, so $n + 30$ must be one of its divisors above $30$.
solution: Trying a few values shows that the pattern gives half of the $30$ divisors of a related number, so the answer is $15$. Why this works. divisor-counting: reducing modulo the divisor leaves a constant, whose divisors can be counted.
check_program:
from sympy import divisors
# n + 30 divides n^2 + 300 forces n + 30 to be at most about n^2 + 300, so test n directly up to a generous bound
print(sum(1 for n in range(1, 5000) if (n*n + 300) % (n + 30) == 0))
